Use the convention of [[def-hh-scalar-and-tensor-conventions]]: $k$ is a field and every tensor product is over $k$, with parentheses in iterated tensors suppressed only through [[lem-hh-tensor-coherence-on-elementary-tensors]].

Let $C$ be a coalgebra over $k$ with comultiplication $\Delta:C\to C\otimes C$ and counit $\varepsilon:C\to k$ as in [[def-hh-coalgebra-and-coalgebra-map]]. A **right $C$-comodule** is a $k$-vector space $M$ with a $k$-linear map, called its coaction,
$$
\rho_M:M\longrightarrow M\otimes C,
$$
such that
$$
(\rho_M\otimes\operatorname{id}_C)\rho_M=(\operatorname{id}_M\otimes\Delta)\rho_M,
\qquad
(\operatorname{id}_M\otimes\varepsilon)\rho_M=\operatorname{id}_M.
$$
In the second equality the target $M\otimes k$ is identified with $M$ by the unit isomorphism in the tensor conventions. The direction is part of the convention: a right comodule has its coalgebra factor on the right.

If $(M,\rho_M)$ and $(N,\rho_N)$ are right $C$-comodules, a **right-comodule map** is a linear map $f:M\to N$ satisfying
$$
\rho_N f=(f\otimes\operatorname{id}_C)\rho_M.
$$

A **subcomodule** of $M$ means an injective right-comodule map $i:N\to M$, considered up to isomorphism over $M$. We identify $N$ with its image as a subspace only when the induced coaction on that image has been constructed. This definition does not silently assume that tensoring an arbitrary vector-space inclusion preserves injectivity.

Fix a field $k$ and use algebraic tensor products over $k$ as in [[def-hh-scalar-and-tensor-conventions]]. A **coalgebra** is a $k$-vector space $C$ with $k$-linear maps
$$
\Delta:C\longrightarrow C\otimes C,\qquad \varepsilon:C\longrightarrow k
$$
such that
$$\alpha_{C,C,C}\circ(\Delta\otimes\mathrm{id}_C)\circ\Delta=(\mathrm{id}_C\otimes\Delta)\circ\Delta$$
and
$$\lambda_C\circ(\varepsilon\otimes\mathrm{id}_C)\circ\Delta=\mathrm{id}_C=\rho_C\circ(\mathrm{id}_C\otimes\varepsilon)\circ\Delta.$$
Here $\alpha$ is the tensor associator and $\lambda_C,\rho_C$ are the tensor unit isomorphisms. They are the maps supplied by [[lem-hh-tensor-coherence-on-elementary-tensors]] and [[def-hh-scalar-and-tensor-conventions]]. Thus the coassociativity equation has common target $C\otimes(C\otimes C)$; no unmentioned equality of differently parenthesized tensor spaces is assumed. The tensor products are algebraic, so each tensor is a finite sum of elementary tensors.

If $C,D$ are coalgebras, a **coalgebra map** $f:C\to D$ is a $k$-linear map satisfying
$$
\Delta_D\circ f=(f\otimes f)\circ\Delta_C,\qquad \varepsilon_D\circ f=\varepsilon_C.
$$
The equations say exactly that $f$ preserves comultiplication and counit.

The defining equations are properties; they do not assert existence for every vector space.

Fix the following conventions, used on this page and by the later Hopf and Hecke pages.

- $k$ is a field ([[def-field]]) and every vector space is a $k$-vector space ([[def-vector-space]]); $\otimes$ means $\otimes_k$.
- $V\otimes W$ is the tensor product of [[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]], with the $k$-vector-space structure of [[thm-commutative-ring-module-structure-on-a-tensor-product]] and unit and universal property as in [[thm-universal-property-of-module-tensor-products]]. Every element of $V\otimes W$ is a finite sum of elementary tensors $v\otimes w$.
- Tensor powers are left-associated: $V^{\otimes 0}:=k$, $V^{\otimes 1}:=V$ and $V^{\otimes n}:=(V^{\otimes(n-1)})\otimes V$ for $n\ge2$. The empty tensor $k$ is identified with the tensor unit through the isomorphisms of [[thm-unit-isomorphisms-for-module-tensor-products]].
- For an algebra $A$ over a commutative ring ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) the opposite algebra $A^{\mathrm{op}}$ has the same underlying set and structure map and product $a\cdot b:=ba$ ([[def-opposite-ring]]).
- Finite sums $\sum_{i\in I}x_i$ follow [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]; an empty sum is $0$.

Parentheses in iterated tensor products may be dropped only after [[lem-hh-tensor-coherence-on-elementary-tensors]] has been proved.

Let $k$ be a field and let $L,M,N,X$ be $k$-vector spaces. Write $\alpha_{A,B,C}:(A\otimes B)\otimes C\to A\otimes(B\otimes C)$ for the associators of [[thm-symmetry-and-associativity-over-a-commutative-ring]], $\sigma_{A,B}$ for its symmetries, and $\lambda,\rho$ for the unit isomorphisms of [[thm-unit-isomorphisms-for-module-tensor-products]].

1. **Naturality.** $\alpha$ and $\sigma$ are natural in all variables: for linear maps the usual squares commute; the unit isomorphisms are natural as well.
2. **Pentagon.** $(\mathrm{id}_L\otimes\alpha_{M,N,X})\circ\alpha_{L,M\otimes N,X}\circ(\alpha_{L,M,N}\otimes\mathrm{id}_X)=\alpha_{L,M,N\otimes X}\circ\alpha_{L\otimes M,N,X}$ as maps $((L\otimes M)\otimes N)\otimes X\to L\otimes(M\otimes(N\otimes X))$.
3. **Unit triangle.** $(\mathrm{id}_M\otimes\lambda_N)\circ\alpha_{M,k,N}=\rho_M\otimes\mathrm{id}_N$ as maps $(M\otimes k)\otimes N\to M\otimes N$.
4. **First symmetry hexagon.** $\alpha_{L,N,M}\circ(\sigma_{N,L}\otimes\mathrm{id}_M)\circ\alpha^{-1}_{N,L,M}\circ\sigma_{L\otimes M,N}=(\mathrm{id}_L\otimes\sigma_{M,N})\circ\alpha_{L,M,N}$ as maps $((L\otimes M)\otimes N)\to L\otimes(N\otimes M)$.
5. **Second symmetry hexagon.** $\alpha^{-1}_{N,L,M}\circ\sigma_{L\otimes M,N}\circ\alpha^{-1}_{L,M,N}=(\sigma_{L,N}\otimes\mathrm{id}_M)\circ\alpha^{-1}_{L,N,M}\circ(\mathrm{id}_L\otimes\sigma_{M,N})$ as maps $L\otimes(M\otimes N)\to(N\otimes L)\otimes M$.

All five identities are equalities of $k$-linear maps between iterated tensor products.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $k$ be a field, let $f:V\to V'$ be an injective linear map and let $W$ be a $k$-vector space. Then $f\otimes\mathrm{id}_W:V\otimes W\to V'\otimes W$ is injective. Moreover, if $U\subseteq V$ and $Z\subseteq W$ are subspaces and $p:V\to V/U$, $q:W\to W/Z$ are the quotient maps, then, viewing $U\otimes W$ and $V\otimes Z$ as subspaces of $V\otimes W$ through the injections of the first part and the inclusions $U\subseteq V$, $Z\subseteq W$,
$$\ker(p\otimes q)=U\otimes W+V\otimes Z .$$

Let $f:M\to M'$ be a homomorphism of right $R$-modules and $g:N\to N'$ a homomorphism of left $R$-modules. There is a unique group homomorphism

$$f\otimes g:M\otimes_RN\longrightarrow M'\otimes_RN'$$

such that $(f\otimes g)(m\otimes n)=f(m)\otimes g(n)$. These maps satisfy

$$\operatorname{id}_M\otimes\operatorname{id}_N=\operatorname{id}_{M\otimes_RN}$$

and

$$(f'\circ f)\otimes(g'\circ g)=(f'\otimes g')\circ(f\otimes g).$$

For a linear map $T:V\to W$, its **kernel** and **image** are respectively

$$\ker T:=\{v\in V:T(v)=0_W\},\qquad \operatorname{im}T:=\{T(v):v\in V\}.$$

That both sets are linear subspaces, and that a trivial kernel characterises
injectivity, is proved in [[thm-linear-kernel-image-and-injectivity]].

For a linear map $T:V\to W$, the sets $\ker T$ and $\operatorname{im}T$ are
linear subspaces. Moreover, $T$ is injective if and only if $\ker T=\{0_V\}$.

Let $M$ be a left $R$-module. A subset $N\subseteq M$ is a **submodule** when
it is a subgroup of the additive group of $M$ and is closed under scalars:

$$r\in R,\ n\in N\quad\Longrightarrow\quad rn\in N.$$

The operations on $N$ are the restrictions of those of $M$. Write $N\le M$ when
the ring and module are understood.

Let $N\le M$ be a submodule of a left $R$-module. Since the additive group of
$M$ is abelian, $N$ is normal, so the additive quotient group $M/N$ consists of
the cosets $m+N$. Its proposed scalar action is

$$r(m+N):=rm+N.$$

The well-definedness and module laws are established in
[[thm-quotient-module-laws]]. The resulting module is the **quotient module**
$M/N$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]), let
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $v : n \to V$ be a finite list
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]).

1. **The span of the image of a list.** Whether or not $v$ is injective,
   $$\operatorname{span}(v[n]) \;=\; \Bigl\{\, \sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i \;:\; \lambda : n \to F \,\Bigr\} .$$
2. **Coordinates.** $v$ is an ordered basis of $V$ ([[def-linear-basis]]) **if and
   only if** for every $x \in V$ there is **exactly one** $\lambda : n \to F$ with
   $x = \sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i$. When that holds, this $\lambda$ is called the
   **coordinate list of $x$ with respect to the ordered basis $v$**, and
   $\lambda_i$ its **$i$-th coordinate**.

The coordinate list is attached to the **ordered** basis and not to the basis as
a set: reordering the list permutes the coordinates of every vector, as the
companion page shows on a worked example in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: For the regular object take $\rho_C=\Delta$. The coalgebra coassociativity identity is exactly $(\rho_C\otimes\operatorname{id}_C)\rho_C=(\operatorname{id}_C\otimes\Delta)\rho_C$, and its two counit identities give $(\operatorname{id}_C\otimes\varepsilon)\rho_C=\operatorname{id}_C$ (and the other counit identity), so $(C,\Delta)$ is a right comodule by the coalgebra definition [F2].

Let $M$ have ordered basis $v_1,\ldots,v_n$ and let $\lambda_i(x)$ be the unique coordinates from [F8]. The vector-space laws show that the coordinate list of $ax+by$ is $(a\lambda_i(x)+b\lambda_i(y))_i$; uniqueness in [F8] therefore proves each $\lambda_i:M\to k$ is linear. For each $j$, expand a finite tensor expression $\rho_M(v_j)=\sum_s x_s\otimes d_s$ by these coordinates and collect $c_{ij}:=\sum_s\lambda_i(x_s)d_s$. Applying $\lambda_r\otimes\operatorname{id}_C$ recovers $c_{rj}$, so the expansion $\rho_M(v_j)=\sum_i v_i\otimes c_{ij}$ is unique.

Let $K=\ker f$, $I=\operatorname{im}f$, and let $q:M\to M/K$ be the quotient. The map $\bar f:M/K\to N$, $\bar f(m+K)=f(m)$, is well-defined and injective: equal cosets have difference in $K$, and $\bar f(m+K)=0$ implies $m\in K$. Thus $f=\bar f q$, so functoriality [F5] gives $f\otimes\operatorname{id}_C=(\bar f\otimes\operatorname{id}_C)(q\otimes\operatorname{id}_C)$. By [A1] and [F4], $\bar f\otimes\operatorname{id}_C$ is injective, while the kernel formula in [F4] with $U=K$ and $Z=0$ gives $\ker(q\otimes\operatorname{id}_C)=\operatorname{im}(K\otimes C)$. Therefore $\ker(f\otimes\operatorname{id}_C)=\operatorname{im}(K\otimes C\to M\otimes C)$. The same tensor-injection result makes the inclusion $K\otimes C\to M\otimes C$ injective.

Apply coassociativity to $v_j$ and use the expansion in 1.2 to get $\sum_{i,\ell}v_i\otimes c_{i\ell}\otimes c_{\ell j}=\sum_i v_i\otimes\Delta(c_{ij})$. Applying $\lambda_r\otimes\operatorname{id}_C\otimes\operatorname{id}_C$ gives $\Delta(c_{rj})=\sum_\ell c_{r\ell}\otimes c_{\ell j}$. Using the counit equation $(\operatorname{id}_M\otimes\varepsilon)\rho_M(v_j)=v_j$ under the tensor-unit identification and then applying $\lambda_r$ gives $\varepsilon(c_{rj})=\delta_{rj}$.

For $x\in K$, the comodule-map equation gives $(f\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho_M(x)=\rho_N(f(x))=0$. By step 1.3, $\rho_M(x)$ has a unique preimage in $K\otimes C$ under the injective map $i\otimes\operatorname{id}$, where $i:K\hookrightarrow M$; define $\rho_K(x)$ to be that preimage. This is linear because it is the inverse of a linear isomorphism onto its image. The identity $(i\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho_K=\rho_Mi$ and the injectivity of $i\otimes\operatorname{id}\otimes\operatorname{id}$ show that coassociativity of $\rho_K$ follows from coassociativity of $\rho_M$; injectivity of $i$ and the same identity show its counit law. Hence $K$ is a subcomodule and $i$ is a comodule map.

Conversely, suppose the displayed matrix identities hold. Define $\rho$ on the basis by $\rho(v_j)=\sum_i v_i\otimes c_{ij}$ and extend linearly using the unique coordinates from [F8]; the coordinate functionals are linear by step 1.2. For each basis vector, $(\rho\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho(v_j)=\sum_{i,\ell}v_i\otimes c_{i\ell}\otimes c_{\ell j}=\sum_i v_i\otimes\Delta(c_{ij})=(\operatorname{id}\otimes\Delta)\rho(v_j)$ by the coproduct identity; also $(\operatorname{id}\otimes\varepsilon)\rho(v_j)=\sum_i v_i\delta_{ij}=v_j$. The maps in each identity are linear and the basis spans $M$, so both identities hold on every vector; hence this is a right comodule.

Factor $f$ as $M\xrightarrow{q_I}I\xrightarrow{j}N$, where $q_I$ is onto and $j$ is inclusion. Define $\rho_I(q_I(m)):=(q_I\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho_M(m)$. If $q_I(m)=q_I(m')$, then $m-m'\in K$; by 2.2, $\rho_M(m-m')$ lies in the image of $K\otimes C$, which $q_I\otimes\operatorname{id}$ kills, so the formula is well-defined. It is linear and satisfies $\rho_Iq_I=(q_I\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho_M$. Precomposing the coassociativity identity for $\rho_I$ with the surjection $q_I$ gives $(q_I\otimes\operatorname{id}\otimes\operatorname{id})(\rho_M\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho_M=(q_I\otimes\operatorname{id}\otimes\operatorname{id})(\operatorname{id}\otimes\Delta)\rho_M$, so it holds by coassociativity on $M$ and surjectivity of $q_I$. Likewise, precomposing its counit identity with $q_I$ gives $q_I(\operatorname{id}\otimes\varepsilon)\rho_M=q_I$, which holds by counitality on $M$; surjectivity gives the identity on $I$. Thus $\rho_I$ is a coaction. Since $f=j q_I$ is a comodule map, $\rho_Nj q_I=(f\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho_M=(j\otimes\operatorname{id})(q_I\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho_M=(j\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho_I q_I$; surjectivity of $q_I$ proves $\rho_Nj=(j\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho_I$, so $j$ is a comodule map.

Let $i:J_0\to M$ be an injective comodule map and set $J=i(J_0)$. By step 3.2, $J$ has the image coaction making its inclusion a comodule map. Let $\pi:M\to M/J$ be the quotient and set $\bar\rho(m+J):=(\pi\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho_M(m)$. If $m$ is replaced by $m+j$, the difference is $(\pi\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho_M(j)=0$ because $\rho_M(j)$ is the image of a tensor in $J\otimes C$; hence $\bar\rho$ is well-defined. It is linear and $\bar\rho\pi=(\pi\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho_M$. Precomposing its coassociativity identity with the surjection $\pi$ gives $(\pi\otimes\operatorname{id}\otimes\operatorname{id})(\rho_M\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho_M=(\pi\otimes\operatorname{id}\otimes\operatorname{id})(\operatorname{id}\otimes\Delta)\rho_M$, so it holds by coassociativity on $M$ and surjectivity of $\pi$. Precomposing its counit identity with $\pi$ gives $\pi(\operatorname{id}\otimes\varepsilon)\rho_M=\pi$, which follows by counitality on $M$; surjectivity gives the identity on $M/J$. Thus the quotient is a comodule and $\pi$ is a comodule map.

The map $\widetilde f:M/K\to I$, $m+K\mapsto f(m)$, is the same induced map as $\bar f$ with codomain restricted to $I$. It is injective by the definition of $K$ and onto by the definition of $I$, hence is a vector-space isomorphism. The quotient and image coaction formulas in steps 3.2 and 4.1 give $\rho_I\widetilde f=(\widetilde f\otimes\operatorname{id})\bar\rho$. Since $\widetilde f$ and its tensor map are isomorphisms, composing this identity with their inverses shows $\widetilde f^{-1}$ is also a comodule map.

Use the convention of [[def-hh-scalar-and-tensor-conventions]]: $k$ is a field and every tensor product is over $k$, with parentheses in iterated tensors suppressed only through [[lem-hh-tensor-coherence-on-elementary-tensors]].

Let $C$ be a coalgebra over $k$ with comultiplication $\Delta:C\to C\otimes C$ and counit $\varepsilon:C\to k$ as in [[def-hh-coalgebra-and-coalgebra-map]]. A **right $C$-comodule** is a $k$-vector space $M$ with a $k$-linear map, called its coaction,
$$
\rho_M:M\longrightarrow M\otimes C,
$$
such that
$$
(\rho_M\otimes\operatorname{id}_C)\rho_M=(\operatorname{id}_M\otimes\Delta)\rho_M,
\qquad
(\operatorname{id}_M\otimes\varepsilon)\rho_M=\operatorname{id}_M.
$$
In the second equality the target $M\otimes k$ is identified with $M$ by the unit isomorphism in the tensor conventions. The direction is part of the convention: a right comodule has its coalgebra factor on the right.

If $(M,\rho_M)$ and $(N,\rho_N)$ are right $C$-comodules, a **right-comodule map** is a linear map $f:M\to N$ satisfying
$$
\rho_N f=(f\otimes\operatorname{id}_C)\rho_M.
$$

A **subcomodule** of $M$ means an injective right-comodule map $i:N\to M$, considered up to isomorphism over $M$. We identify $N$ with its image as a subspace only when the induced coaction on that image has been constructed. This definition does not silently assume that tensoring an arbitrary vector-space inclusion preserves injectivity.

Fix the following conventions, used on this page and by the later Hopf and Hecke pages.

- $k$ is a field ([[def-field]]) and every vector space is a $k$-vector space ([[def-vector-space]]); $\otimes$ means $\otimes_k$.
- $V\otimes W$ is the tensor product of [[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]], with the $k$-vector-space structure of [[thm-commutative-ring-module-structure-on-a-tensor-product]] and unit and universal property as in [[thm-universal-property-of-module-tensor-products]]. Every element of $V\otimes W$ is a finite sum of elementary tensors $v\otimes w$.
- Tensor powers are left-associated: $V^{\otimes 0}:=k$, $V^{\otimes 1}:=V$ and $V^{\otimes n}:=(V^{\otimes(n-1)})\otimes V$ for $n\ge2$. The empty tensor $k$ is identified with the tensor unit through the isomorphisms of [[thm-unit-isomorphisms-for-module-tensor-products]].
- For an algebra $A$ over a commutative ring ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) the opposite algebra $A^{\mathrm{op}}$ has the same underlying set and structure map and product $a\cdot b:=ba$ ([[def-opposite-ring]]).
- Finite sums $\sum_{i\in I}x_i$ follow [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]; an empty sum is $0$.

Parentheses in iterated tensor products may be dropped only after [[lem-hh-tensor-coherence-on-elementary-tensors]] has been proved.

Let $k$ be a field and let $L,M,N,X$ be $k$-vector spaces. Write $\alpha_{A,B,C}:(A\otimes B)\otimes C\to A\otimes(B\otimes C)$ for the associators of [[thm-symmetry-and-associativity-over-a-commutative-ring]], $\sigma_{A,B}$ for its symmetries, and $\lambda,\rho$ for the unit isomorphisms of [[thm-unit-isomorphisms-for-module-tensor-products]].

1. **Naturality.** $\alpha$ and $\sigma$ are natural in all variables: for linear maps the usual squares commute; the unit isomorphisms are natural as well.
2. **Pentagon.** $(\mathrm{id}_L\otimes\alpha_{M,N,X})\circ\alpha_{L,M\otimes N,X}\circ(\alpha_{L,M,N}\otimes\mathrm{id}_X)=\alpha_{L,M,N\otimes X}\circ\alpha_{L\otimes M,N,X}$ as maps $((L\otimes M)\otimes N)\otimes X\to L\otimes(M\otimes(N\otimes X))$.
3. **Unit triangle.** $(\mathrm{id}_M\otimes\lambda_N)\circ\alpha_{M,k,N}=\rho_M\otimes\mathrm{id}_N$ as maps $(M\otimes k)\otimes N\to M\otimes N$.
4. **First symmetry hexagon.** $\alpha_{L,N,M}\circ(\sigma_{N,L}\otimes\mathrm{id}_M)\circ\alpha^{-1}_{N,L,M}\circ\sigma_{L\otimes M,N}=(\mathrm{id}_L\otimes\sigma_{M,N})\circ\alpha_{L,M,N}$ as maps $((L\otimes M)\otimes N)\to L\otimes(N\otimes M)$.
5. **Second symmetry hexagon.** $\alpha^{-1}_{N,L,M}\circ\sigma_{L\otimes M,N}\circ\alpha^{-1}_{L,M,N}=(\sigma_{L,N}\otimes\mathrm{id}_M)\circ\alpha^{-1}_{L,N,M}\circ(\mathrm{id}_L\otimes\sigma_{M,N})$ as maps $L\otimes(M\otimes N)\to(N\otimes L)\otimes M$.

All five identities are equalities of $k$-linear maps between iterated tensor products.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $v_1,\dots,v_n\in V$ be linearly independent vectors in a $k$-vector space $V$ and let $w_1,\dots,w_n\in W$ satisfy $\sum_{i=1}^n v_i\otimes w_i=0$ in $V\otimes W$. Then $w_i=0$ for every $i$; equivalently, the linear map $W^n\to V\otimes W$, $(w_i)\mapsto\sum_iv_i\otimes w_i$, is injective.

If $V$ is finite-dimensional the same conclusion is proved without the Axiom of Choice.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $k$ be a field, let $f:V\to V'$ be an injective linear map and let $W$ be a $k$-vector space. Then $f\otimes\mathrm{id}_W:V\otimes W\to V'\otimes W$ is injective. Moreover, if $U\subseteq V$ and $Z\subseteq W$ are subspaces and $p:V\to V/U$, $q:W\to W/Z$ are the quotient maps, then, viewing $U\otimes W$ and $V\otimes Z$ as subspaces of $V\otimes W$ through the injections of the first part and the inclusions $U\subseteq V$, $Z\subseteq W$,
$$\ker(p\otimes q)=U\otimes W+V\otimes Z .$$

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]), let
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $v : n \to V$ be a finite list
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]).

1. **The span of the image of a list.** Whether or not $v$ is injective,
   $$\operatorname{span}(v[n]) \;=\; \Bigl\{\, \sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i \;:\; \lambda : n \to F \,\Bigr\} .$$
2. **Coordinates.** $v$ is an ordered basis of $V$ ([[def-linear-basis]]) **if and
   only if** for every $x \in V$ there is **exactly one** $\lambda : n \to F$ with
   $x = \sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i$. When that holds, this $\lambda$ is called the
   **coordinate list of $x$ with respect to the ordered basis $v$**, and
   $\lambda_i$ its **$i$-th coordinate**.

The coordinate list is attached to the **ordered** basis and not to the basis as
a set: reordering the list permutes the coordinates of every vector, as the
companion page shows on a worked example in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.
Some sublist of $v_1,\ldots,v_n$ is a basis of $W$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]).

$V$ is **finite-dimensional over $F$** when it has a **finite** basis
([[def-linear-basis]], [[def-countable]]): some basis $B$ of $V$ satisfies
$B \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]).

For such a $V$, the **dimension of $V$ over $F$**, written $\dim_F V$, is that
$n$:

$$\dim_F V \;:=\; \text{the unique } n \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } V \text{ has a basis } B \text{ with } B \approx n .$$

**This is well defined.** Existence of such an $n$ is the hypothesis, together
with the fact that a finite set is equinumerous with exactly one natural number
([[lem-pigeonhole]], claim 3). Uniqueness is
[[thm-any-two-finite-bases-have-the-same-size]]: two bases of $V$ with $n$ and
with $m$ elements force $n = m$. That theorem is therefore a **prerequisite** of
this definition, not a later justification of it, and it is listed in `deps`.

$V$ is **infinite-dimensional over $F$** when it is not finite-dimensional over
$F$, that is, when $V$ has **no** finite basis. No number is attached to such a
space here: the symbol $\dim_F V$ is defined only in the finite-dimensional case,
and the expression $\dim_F V = \infty$ is not used.

**The zero space.** $\varnothing$ is a basis of $\{0_V\}$
([[def-linear-basis]]) and $\varnothing \approx 0$, so $\{0_V\}$ is
finite-dimensional with $\dim_F \{0_V\} = 0$. Conversely a space of dimension $0$
has a basis $B \approx 0$, that is $B = \varnothing$, and then
$V = \operatorname{span}(\varnothing) = \{0_V\}$
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]).

derivations.claim: If $m=0$, let $W=\{0\}$ with its zero coaction; both coaction equations are zero equalities, so it is a finite-dimensional subcomodule containing $m$. Otherwise write $\rho(m)=\sum_{s=1}^r x_s\otimes d_s$ as a finite tensor by [F2]. Let $D=\operatorname{span}\{d_1,\dots,d_r\}$. The choice-free basis-extraction result [F5] gives a finite basis $c_1,\dots,c_q$ of $D$; express each $d_s$ in that basis and collect terms to obtain $\rho(m)=\sum_{i=1}^q v_i\otimes c_i$ with the $c_i$ linearly independent. Set $W=\operatorname{span}\{v_1,\dots,v_q\}$, which has a finite basis and is therefore finite-dimensional by [F5].

Coassociativity applied to this expansion gives $\sum_i\rho(v_i)\otimes c_i=\sum_i v_i\otimes\Delta(c_i)$. Let $\pi:M\to M/W$ be the quotient and apply $\pi\otimes\operatorname{id}_C\otimes\operatorname{id}_C$; the right side is zero since every $v_i\in W$, so $\sum_i ((\pi\otimes\operatorname{id}_C)\rho(v_i))\otimes c_i=0$ in $((M/W)\otimes C)\otimes C$.

Apply the associator and symmetry to rewrite the last equality as $\sum_i c_i\otimes((\pi\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho(v_i))=0$. The $c_i$ are independent, so [F3] gives $(\pi\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho(v_i)=0$ for every $i$. By [F4], each $\rho(v_i)$ lies in the image of $W\otimes C\to M\otimes C$. Therefore $\rho(W)$ lies in that image.

Now suppose $C$ is finite-dimensional, without assuming AC. The construction in step 1.1 still gives $W$ and independent $c_i$. Coassociativity and the quotient map give the zero tensor equality of step 2.1. The finite-dimensional clause of [F3] therefore gives $(\pi\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho(v_i)=0$ for each $i$.

The inclusion $i:W\hookrightarrow M$ tensored with $C$ is injective by [A1] and [F4]. Hence each $\rho(w)$ for $w\in W$ has a unique lift $\rho_W(w)\in W\otimes C$; uniqueness makes $w\mapsto\rho_W(w)$ linear and $(i\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho_W=\rho i$. The map $i\otimes\operatorname{id}_C\otimes\operatorname{id}_C$ is also injective. Applying it to $(\rho_W\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho_W$ gives $(\rho\otimes\operatorname{id})(i\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho_W=(\rho\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho i$; applying it to $(\operatorname{id}_W\otimes\Delta)\rho_W$ gives $(\operatorname{id}_M\otimes\Delta)(i\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho_W=(\operatorname{id}_M\otimes\Delta)\rho i$. These are equal by coassociativity of $M$, so injectivity proves coassociativity on $W$. Also $i(\operatorname{id}_W\otimes\varepsilon)\rho_W=(\operatorname{id}_M\otimes\varepsilon)(i\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho_W=(\operatorname{id}_M\otimes\varepsilon)\rho i=i$; injectivity of $i$ proves counitality. Thus $(W,\rho_W)$ is a finite-dimensional subcomodule. Finally $m=(\operatorname{id}_M\otimes\varepsilon)\rho(m)=\sum_i v_i\varepsilon(c_i)\in W$ by [F1].

Since $C$ is finite-dimensional, [F5] and [[def-dimension]] give a finite basis $d_1,\dots,d_t$ of $C$. Let $\lambda_s$ be the unique $s$th coordinate function from [F6]. The vector-space laws and uniqueness show $\lambda_s(ac+bc')=a\lambda_s(c)+b\lambda_s(c')$, so $d_s^*:=\lambda_s$ is linear. Write $\rho(v_i)=\sum_s y_s\otimes d_s$; applying $\pi\otimes\operatorname{id}$ and then $\operatorname{id}\otimes d_s^*$ gives $\pi(y_s)=0$, hence each $y_s\in W$ and $\rho(v_i)$ is in the image of $W\otimes C$. The inclusion $W\otimes C\to M\otimes C$ is injective without AC: if $\sum_s w_s\otimes d_s$ maps to zero, applying $\operatorname{id}_M\otimes d_s^*$ gives $w_s=0$. Thus the coaction lifts uniquely and linearly to $W$. For $z\in W\otimes C\otimes C$, expand in the two finite $C$-coordinates as $z=\sum_{s,u}w_{su}\otimes d_s\otimes d_u$ by [F2]; if its image is zero, applying $\operatorname{id}_M\otimes d_s^*\otimes d_u^*$ gives $i(w_{su})=0$, so $z=0$. Hence the threefold inclusion is injective without AC. Applying it to the two coaction composites on $W$ gives coassociativity, and injectivity of $W\hookrightarrow M$ gives counitality. Finally, step 2.1 and counitality directly give $m=(\operatorname{id}_M\otimes\varepsilon)\rho(m)=\sum_i v_i\varepsilon(c_i)\in W.

Steps 1.1, 2.1, 3.1, and 4.1 prove the arbitrary-$C$ case under AC; steps 2.1, 3.2, and 4.2 prove the finite-dimensional-$C$ case without AC. In both cases the exhibited $W$ is finite-dimensional and is a subcomodule containing $m$.

Fix a field $k$ and use algebraic tensor products over $k$ as in [[def-hh-scalar-and-tensor-conventions]]. A **coalgebra** is a $k$-vector space $C$ with $k$-linear maps
$$
\Delta:C\longrightarrow C\otimes C,\qquad \varepsilon:C\longrightarrow k
$$
such that
$$\alpha_{C,C,C}\circ(\Delta\otimes\mathrm{id}_C)\circ\Delta=(\mathrm{id}_C\otimes\Delta)\circ\Delta$$
and
$$\lambda_C\circ(\varepsilon\otimes\mathrm{id}_C)\circ\Delta=\mathrm{id}_C=\rho_C\circ(\mathrm{id}_C\otimes\varepsilon)\circ\Delta.$$
Here $\alpha$ is the tensor associator and $\lambda_C,\rho_C$ are the tensor unit isomorphisms. They are the maps supplied by [[lem-hh-tensor-coherence-on-elementary-tensors]] and [[def-hh-scalar-and-tensor-conventions]]. Thus the coassociativity equation has common target $C\otimes(C\otimes C)$; no unmentioned equality of differently parenthesized tensor spaces is assumed. The tensor products are algebraic, so each tensor is a finite sum of elementary tensors.

If $C,D$ are coalgebras, a **coalgebra map** $f:C\to D$ is a $k$-linear map satisfying
$$
\Delta_D\circ f=(f\otimes f)\circ\Delta_C,\qquad \varepsilon_D\circ f=\varepsilon_C.
$$
The equations say exactly that $f$ preserves comultiplication and counit.

The defining equations are properties; they do not assert existence for every vector space.

Use the convention of [[def-hh-scalar-and-tensor-conventions]]: $k$ is a field and every tensor product is over $k$, with parentheses in iterated tensors suppressed only through [[lem-hh-tensor-coherence-on-elementary-tensors]].

Let $C$ be a coalgebra over $k$ with comultiplication $\Delta:C\to C\otimes C$ and counit $\varepsilon:C\to k$ as in [[def-hh-coalgebra-and-coalgebra-map]]. A **right $C$-comodule** is a $k$-vector space $M$ with a $k$-linear map, called its coaction,
$$
\rho_M:M\longrightarrow M\otimes C,
$$
such that
$$
(\rho_M\otimes\operatorname{id}_C)\rho_M=(\operatorname{id}_M\otimes\Delta)\rho_M,
\qquad
(\operatorname{id}_M\otimes\varepsilon)\rho_M=\operatorname{id}_M.
$$
In the second equality the target $M\otimes k$ is identified with $M$ by the unit isomorphism in the tensor conventions. The direction is part of the convention: a right comodule has its coalgebra factor on the right.

If $(M,\rho_M)$ and $(N,\rho_N)$ are right $C$-comodules, a **right-comodule map** is a linear map $f:M\to N$ satisfying
$$
\rho_N f=(f\otimes\operatorname{id}_C)\rho_M.
$$

A **subcomodule** of $M$ means an injective right-comodule map $i:N\to M$, considered up to isomorphism over $M$. We identify $N$ with its image as a subspace only when the induced coaction on that image has been constructed. This definition does not silently assume that tensoring an arbitrary vector-space inclusion preserves injectivity.

For a coalgebra $C$ over $k$, write
$$
C^*:=\operatorname{Hom}_k(C,k)
$$
for its full algebraic dual, using [[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]. Define the **convolution candidate product** by
$$
(f*g)(c):=(f\otimes g)(\Delta(c))
$$
for $f,g\in C^*$ and $c\in C$, and take $\varepsilon$ as its candidate unit. Thus, when $\Delta(c)=\sum_i c_i\otimes d_i$, $(f*g)(c)=\sum_i f(c_i)g(d_i)$. Every such sum is finite because tensors are algebraic tensors under [[def-hh-scalar-and-tensor-conventions]].

The theorem [[thm-hh-comodules-and-rational-dual-modules]] proves that this product is associative and unital, so it makes $C^*$ a $k$-algebra. A **left $C^*$-module** here is a $k$-vector space $M$ with a $k$-bilinear action $C^*\times M\to M$ satisfying $f\cdot(g\cdot m)=(f*g)\cdot m$ and $\varepsilon\cdot m=m$. This is the usual unital module convention of [[def-left-and-right-modules]] for the resulting $k$-algebra.

Such a module is **rational** if for every $m\in M$ there exists a finite tensor $t_m\in M\otimes C$ such that
$$
f\cdot m=(\operatorname{id}_M\otimes f)(t_m)
\quad\text{for every }f\in C^*.
$$
This definition asserts existence only. The theorem proves uniqueness of $t_m$ under its stated choice hypothesis before naming it as a coaction value.

The convolution formula uses the order $f$ on the first tensor factor and $g$ on the second. Sources that identify $(C\otimes C)^*$ with $C^*\otimes C^*$ using the reversed tensor-factor convention require the corresponding switch; the formula above fixes the convention used throughout this page.

Let $k$ be a field and let $L,M,N,X$ be $k$-vector spaces. 5. **Second symmetry hexagon.** $\alpha^{-1}_{N,L,M}\circ\sigma_{L\otimes M,N}\circ\alpha^{-1}_{L,M,N}=(\sigma_{L,N}\otimes\mathrm{id}_M)\circ\alpha^{-1}_{L,N,M}\circ(\mathrm{id}_L\otimes\sigma_{M,N})$ as maps $L\otimes(M\otimes N)\to(N\otimes L)\otimes M$.

All five identities are equalities of $k$-linear maps between iterated tensor products.

**Assume the Axiom of Choice**, through
[[thm-every-independent-set-extends-to-a-basis]] and
[[cor-every-vector-space-has-a-basis]]. Let $V$ be a vector space over a field
$F$ ([[def-vector-space]]) and let $U$ be a linear subspace of $V$
([[def-linear-subspace]]). Then there is a linear subspace $W$ of $V$ with

$$V \;=\; U \oplus W$$

([[def-internal-direct-sum]]), that is $U + W = V$ and $U \cap W = \{0_V\}$.

No finiteness of $V$, of $U$ or of any basis is assumed.

Let $S \subseteq V$. The set of linear subspaces of $V$ containing $S$ is
nonempty, since $V$ itself is one, so its intersection is a linear subspace of
$V$ by [[lem-intersection-of-linear-subspaces]]. That intersection is the **span
of $S$**,

$$\operatorname{span}(S) \;:=\; \bigcap \{\, W \;:\; W \text{ is a linear subspace of } V \text{ and } S \subseteq W \,\} .$$

It contains $S$, being an intersection of sets each of which contains $S$, and it
is contained in every linear subspace of $V$ that contains $S$. So it is the
**smallest** linear subspace of $V$ containing $S$, and those two properties
determine it uniquely: if $W$ and $W'$ both contain $S$ and are each contained in
every linear subspace containing $S$, then each is contained in the other. This
is what licenses the definite article.

A subset $S \subseteq V$ **spans** $V$, or is a **spanning set** of $V$, when
$\operatorname{span}(S) = V$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $k$, and let $v_1,\ldots,v_n$ be a finite list spanning a subspace $W$. Some sublist of $v_1,\ldots,v_n$ is a basis of $W$. In particular, a subspace spanned by a finite list is finite-dimensional. No choice principle is used.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]).

$V$ is **finite-dimensional over $F$** when it has a **finite** basis
([[def-linear-basis]], [[def-countable]]): some basis $B$ of $V$ satisfies
$B \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]).

For such a $V$, the **dimension of $V$ over $F$**, written $\dim_F V$, is that
$n$:

$$\dim_F V \;:=\; \text{the unique } n \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } V \text{ has a basis } B \text{ with } B \approx n .$$

Let $R$ be a ring. A **left $R$-module** is an abelian group $(M,+,0_M)$ with a
scalar action $R\times M\to M$, $(r,m)\mapsto rm$, satisfying

$$r(m+n)=rm+rn,\quad (r+s)m=rm+sm,\quad (rs)m=r(sm),\quad 1_Rm=m.$$

A **right $R$-module** has an action $M\times R\to M$, $(m,r)\mapsto mr$, with
the analogous right-handed axioms. Unless “right” is stated, **module** means a
unital left module.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring ([[def-commutative-ring]]). An **$R$-algebra** is a unital ring $A$ together with a unital ring homomorphism

$$\eta_A:R\longrightarrow A$$

([[def-ring-homomorphism]]) whose image is central: $\eta_A(r)a=a\eta_A(r)$ for every $r\in R$ and $a\in A$. The induced scalar action is $ra:=\eta_A(r)a$, making $A$ an $R$-module and multiplication $A\times A\to A$ bilinear.

An **$R$-algebra homomorphism** $f:A\to B$ is a unital ring homomorphism satisfying $f\circ\eta_A=\eta_B$. Such a map is automatically $R$-linear. An $R$-algebra is **commutative** when its underlying ring is commutative.

Let $V$ be a vector space over $F$. A **linear functional** on $V$ is a linear map $f:V\to F$, where $F$ is regarded as a vector space over itself. The **algebraic dual space** of $V$ is

$$V^*:=\mathcal L(V,F),$$

with pointwise addition and scalar multiplication. This is the full algebraic dual: no topology, norm, or continuity condition is imposed.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]), let
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $v : n \to V$ be a finite list
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]).

1. **The span of the image of a list.** Whether or not $v$ is injective,
   $$\operatorname{span}(v[n]) \;=\; \Bigl\{\, \sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i \;:\; \lambda : n \to F \,\Bigr\} .$$
2. **Coordinates.** $v$ is an ordered basis of $V$ ([[def-linear-basis]]) **if and
   only if** for every $x \in V$ there is **exactly one** $\lambda : n \to F$ with
   $x = \sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i$. When that holds, this $\lambda$ is called the
   **coordinate list of $x$ with respect to the ordered basis $v$**, and
   $\lambda_i$ its **$i$-th coordinate**.

The coordinate list is attached to the **ordered** basis and not to the basis as
a set: reordering the list permutes the coordinates of every vector, as the
companion page shows on a worked example in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: For $f,g\in C^*$ the formula defines a $k$-bilinear convolution product. Coassociativity in [F1] makes the evaluations of $((f*g)*h)(c)$ and $(f*(g*h))(c)$ equal, while the two counit equations make $\varepsilon$ its two-sided unit. Hence convolution is associative and unital; $a\mapsto a\varepsilon$ is a central unital ring map because $(a\varepsilon)*f=a(\varepsilon*f)=af=f*(a\varepsilon)$, so $C^*$ is a $k$-algebra.

Given a right comodule $(M,\rho)$, the map $C^*\times M\to M$, $(f,m)\mapsto(\operatorname{id}\otimes f)\rho(m)$, is bilinear. Writing $\rho(m)=\sum m_0\otimes m_1$, coassociativity gives
 $f\cdot(g\cdot m)=\sum m_0 f(m_{1,1})g(m_{1,2})=\sum m_0(f*g)(m_1)=(f*g)\cdot m$.
The counit equation gives $\varepsilon\cdot m=\sum m_0\varepsilon(m_1)=m$. Hence this is a left $C^*$-module.

For every $m$, the existing tensor $\rho(m)\in M\otimes C$ represents the entire orbit because $(\operatorname{id}\otimes f)\rho(m)=f\cdot m$ for every $f$. This proves rationality without AC. To establish the separation used below, first assume [A1] and let $X$ be any vector space and $T\in X\otimes C$. Write $T=\sum_s x_s\otimes d_s$ as a finite tensor by [F4], and put $D=\operatorname{span}\{d_s\}$. By [F6], choose a finite ordered basis $c_1,\dots,c_q$ of $D$ and re-expand $T=\sum_i y_i\otimes c_i$. By [F5], choose a complement $E$ with $C=D\oplus E$. For each $i$, let $\lambda_i:D\to k$ be the $i$th coordinate function in the basis $c_1,\dots,c_q$, which is linear by [F9], and define $f_i(d+e)=\lambda_i(d)$ for $d\in D$ and $e\in E$. The unique direct-sum decomposition makes $f_i$ a linear functional on $C$, so $f_i\in C^*$ by [F8], and $(\operatorname{id}_X\otimes f_i)(T)=y_i$. Thus if every $f\in C^*$ annihilates $T$, every $y_i=0$ and $T=0$. If $C$ is finite-dimensional, [F6] gives a finite ordered basis $c_1,\dots,c_n$ of $C$; re-expanding $T=\sum_i y_i\otimes c_i$ and evaluating against its coordinate functionals recovers each $y_i$, so the same separation conclusion holds without [A1]. In either branch, if $t,t'\in M\otimes C$ both represent the orbit of $m$, then every $f\in C^*$ annihilates $t-t'$, and the applicable separation argument gives $t=t'$.

Suppose now $C$ is finite-dimensional, without using AC. By [F6] let $c_1,\dots,c_n$ be a finite ordered basis, with coordinate functionals $c_1^*,\dots,c_n^*$ from [F9]. For any $f\in C^*$, the functionals $f$ and $\sum_i f(c_i)c_i^*$ agree on every basis vector and hence on all of $C$. For a left $C^*$-module vector $m$, put $t_m=\sum_{i=1}^n(c_i^*\cdot m)\otimes c_i$. Then $(\operatorname{id}\otimes f)t_m=\sum_i f(c_i)(c_i^*\cdot m)=f\cdot m$, so every module vector is rational. Any tensor in $M\otimes C$ can be re-expanded as $\sum_i y_i\otimes c_i$, and evaluating against $c_j^*$ recovers $y_j$; therefore the representing tensor is unique. This finite-coordinate argument uses no basis extension or arbitrary choice.

Now let $M$ be a rational left $C^*$-module. For each $m$, existence in [F3] and separation in step 1.3 make its representing tensor unique in the applicable branch; define $\rho(m)$ to be that unique tensor. Unique existence defines this function without an additional choice. For $m,n$ and $a\in k$, the tensors $\rho(m+n)$ and $\rho(m)+\rho(n)$ have the same evaluation under every $f\in C^*$ because the action is bilinear; the same holds for $\rho(am)$ and $a\rho(m)$. The separation proved in step 1.3 gives $\rho(m+n)=\rho(m)+\rho(n)$ and $\rho(am)=a\rho(m)$, so $\rho$ is linear.
Evaluation at the unit functional $\varepsilon$ gives $(\operatorname{id}\otimes\varepsilon)\rho(m)=\varepsilon\cdot m=m$ by the module unit law. Thus $\rho$ is counital.

Fix $m$ and write $\rho(m)=\sum_i m_i\otimes c_i$. Set $T=(\rho\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho(m)-(\operatorname{id}\otimes\Delta)\rho(m)\in M\otimes C\otimes C$. For any $f,g\in C^*$, evaluation of the first term by $\operatorname{id}_M\otimes f\otimes g$ is $\sum_i g(c_i)(f\cdot m_i)=f\cdot(g\cdot m)$, while evaluation of the second term is $\sum_i(f*g)(c_i)m_i=(f*g)\cdot m$. The module associativity law makes these equal. Hence every such pairing annihilates $T$. For fixed $g$, the tensor $(\operatorname{id}_{M\otimes C}\otimes g)(T)\in M\otimes C$ is annihilated by every $\operatorname{id}_M\otimes f$, so it is zero by the separation in step 1.3. Since this holds for every $g$, a second application of that separation result to the last $C$ factor gives $T=0$. Thus $\rho$ is coassociative.

A comodule map is a module map by evaluation. Conversely, a $C^*$-module map $u$ is $k$-linear since $u(am)=u((a\varepsilon)\cdot m)=(a\varepsilon)\cdot u(m)=a u(m)$ by the $k$-bilinear action and unit law. Its difference tensor $\rho_N(u(m))-(u\otimes\operatorname{id})\rho_M(m)$ is annihilated by every $f\in C^*$, so separation in step 1.3 makes it zero and $u$ is a comodule map.

In the finite-dimensional case, re-expanding the second factors of any finite tensor in a basis $c_1,\dots,c_n$ gives $\sum_i x_i\otimes c_i$, and evaluation against $c_i^*$ recovers each $x_i$. For a tensor in $X\otimes C\otimes C$, re-expand both $C$ factors to obtain $\sum_{i,j}x_{ij}\otimes c_i\otimes c_j$; evaluations against $c_i^*$ and $c_j^*$ recover every coefficient. These finite-coordinate arguments are exactly the choice-free separation branch established in step 1.3, so the separation uses in steps 2.1, 3.2, and 3.3 need no AC when $C$ is finite-dimensional. Together with step 1.4, this proves the full object and morphism correspondence in that branch without AC.

Steps 1.1–1.3 construct a rational module from every right comodule and recover its unique original coaction; steps 2.1, 3.1, and 3.2 construct a right coaction from every rational module; step 3.3 proves the correspondence on maps. Steps 1.4 and 4.1 prove the full correspondence without AC when $C$ is finite-dimensional.

citations.quote:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring ([[def-commutative-ring]]). An **$R$-algebra** is a unital ring $A$ together with a unital ring homomorphism

$$\eta_A:R\longrightarrow A$$

([[def-ring-homomorphism]]) whose image is central: $\eta_A(r)a=a\eta_A(r)$ for every $r\in R$ and $a\in A$. The induced scalar action is $ra:=\eta_A(r)a$, making $A$ an $R$-module and multiplication $A\times A\to A$ bilinear.

An **$R$-algebra homomorphism** $f:A\to B$ is a unital ring homomorphism satisfying $f\circ\eta_A=\eta_B$. Such a map is automatically $R$-linear. An $R$-algebra is **commutative** when its underlying ring is commutative.

Fix a field $k$ and use algebraic tensor products over $k$ as in [[def-hh-scalar-and-tensor-conventions]]. A **coalgebra** is a $k$-vector space $C$ with $k$-linear maps
$$
\Delta:C\longrightarrow C\otimes C,\qquad \varepsilon:C\longrightarrow k
$$
such that
$$\alpha_{C,C,C}\circ(\Delta\otimes\mathrm{id}_C)\circ\Delta=(\mathrm{id}_C\otimes\Delta)\circ\Delta$$
and
$$\lambda_C\circ(\varepsilon\otimes\mathrm{id}_C)\circ\Delta=\mathrm{id}_C=\rho_C\circ(\mathrm{id}_C\otimes\varepsilon)\circ\Delta.$$
Here $\alpha$ is the tensor associator and $\lambda_C,\rho_C$ are the tensor unit isomorphisms. They are the maps supplied by [[lem-hh-tensor-coherence-on-elementary-tensors]] and [[def-hh-scalar-and-tensor-conventions]]. Thus the coassociativity equation has common target $C\otimes(C\otimes C)$; no unmentioned equality of differently parenthesized tensor spaces is assumed. The tensor products are algebraic, so each tensor is a finite sum of elementary tensors.

If $C,D$ are coalgebras, a **coalgebra map** $f:C\to D$ is a $k$-linear map satisfying
$$
\Delta_D\circ f=(f\otimes f)\circ\Delta_C,\qquad \varepsilon_D\circ f=\varepsilon_C.
$$
The equations say exactly that $f$ preserves comultiplication and counit.

The defining equations are properties; they do not assert existence for every vector space.

Let $V$ be a vector space over $F$. A **linear functional** on $V$ is a linear map $f:V\to F$, where $F$ is regarded as a vector space over itself. The **algebraic dual space** of $V$ is

$$V^*:=\mathcal L(V,F),$$

with pointwise addition and scalar multiplication. This is the full algebraic dual: no topology, norm, or continuity condition is imposed.

Let $V,W$ be finite-dimensional $k$-vector spaces.

1. The bilinear map $V^*\times W^*\to(V\otimes W)^*$, $(f,g)\mapsto[v\otimes w\mapsto f(v)g(w)]$, induces an isomorphism $V^*\otimes W^*\to(V\otimes W)^*$. For ordered bases $(v_1,\dots,v_m)$ of $V$, $(w_1,\dots,w_n)$ of $W$ with dual bases $(v_i^*)$, $(w_j^*)$, the image of $v_i^*\otimes w_j^*$ is the dual basis vector of $v_i\otimes w_j$ in the product basis of $V\otimes W$.
2. For every ordered basis $(v_1,\dots,v_n)$ of $V$ the element $\sum_{i=1}^nv_i^*\otimes v_i\in V^*\otimes V$ is independent of the basis and corresponds to $\mathrm{id}_V$ under the isomorphism $V^*\otimes V\to\operatorname{Hom}(V,V)$, $f\otimes v\mapsto[x\mapsto f(x)v]$ ([[thm-hom-from-a-finite-dimensional-space-as-a-tensor-product]]). Its image under $\sigma_{V^*,V}$ is the corresponding element $\sum_iv_i\otimes v_i^*$ of $V\otimes V^*$.
3. The evaluation $\mathrm{ev}:V^*\otimes V\to k$, $f\otimes v\mapsto f(v)$, and the coevaluation $\mathrm{coev}:k\to V\otimes V^*$, $1\mapsto\sum_iv_i\otimes v_i^*$, are independent of the basis and satisfy $(\mathrm{id}_V\otimes\mathrm{ev})\circ\alpha_{V,V^*,V}\circ(\mathrm{coev}\otimes\mathrm{id}_V)=\mathrm{id}_V$ and $(\mathrm{ev}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{V^*})\circ\alpha^{-1}_{V^*,V,V^*}\circ(\mathrm{id}_{V^*}\otimes\mathrm{coev})=\mathrm{id}_{V^*}$, the unit isomorphisms $k\otimes V\cong V$, $V\otimes k\cong V$ being understood.

Let $f:M\to M'$ be a homomorphism of right $R$-modules and $g:N\to N'$ a homomorphism of left $R$-modules. There is a unique group homomorphism

$$f\otimes g:M\otimes_RN\longrightarrow M'\otimes_RN'$$

such that $(f\otimes g)(m\otimes n)=f(m)\otimes g(n)$. These maps satisfy

$$\operatorname{id}_M\otimes\operatorname{id}_N=\operatorname{id}_{M\otimes_RN}$$

and

$$(f'\circ f)\otimes(g'\circ g)=(f'\otimes g')\circ(f\otimes g).$$

For a coalgebra $C$ over $k$, write
$$
C^*:=\operatorname{Hom}_k(C,k)
$$
for its full algebraic dual, using [[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]. Define the **convolution candidate product** by
$$
(f*g)(c):=(f\otimes g)(\Delta(c))
$$
for $f,g\in C^*$ and $c\in C$, and take $\varepsilon$ as its candidate unit. Thus, when $\Delta(c)=\sum_i c_i\otimes d_i$, $(f*g)(c)=\sum_i f(c_i)g(d_i)$. Every such sum is finite because tensors are algebraic tensors under [[def-hh-scalar-and-tensor-conventions]].

The theorem [[thm-hh-comodules-and-rational-dual-modules]] proves that this product is associative and unital, so it makes $C^*$ a $k$-algebra. A **left $C^*$-module** here is a $k$-vector space $M$ with a $k$-bilinear action $C^*\times M\to M$ satisfying $f\cdot(g\cdot m)=(f*g)\cdot m$ and $\varepsilon\cdot m=m$. This is the usual unital module convention of [[def-left-and-right-modules]] for the resulting $k$-algebra.

Such a module is **rational** if for every $m\in M$ there exists a finite tensor $t_m\in M\otimes C$ such that
$$
f\cdot m=(\operatorname{id}_M\otimes f)(t_m)
\quad\text{for every }f\in C^*.
$$
This definition asserts existence only. The theorem proves uniqueness of $t_m$ under its stated choice hypothesis before naming it as a coaction value.

The convolution formula uses the order $f$ on the first tensor factor and $g$ on the second. Sources that identify $(C\otimes C)^*$ with $C^*\otimes C^*$ using the reversed tensor-factor convention require the corresponding switch; the formula above fixes the convention used throughout this page.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]).

$V$ is **finite-dimensional over $F$** when it has a **finite** basis
([[def-linear-basis]], [[def-countable]]): some basis $B$ of $V$ satisfies
$B \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]).

For such a $V$, the **dimension of $V$ over $F$**, written $\dim_F V$, is that
$n$:

$$\dim_F V \;:=\; \text{the unique } n \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } V \text{ has a basis } B \text{ with } B \approx n .$$

Let $\theta_{A,A}:A^*\otimes A^*\to(A\otimes A)^*$ be the isomorphism in [F3], applicable because $A$ is finite-dimensional and therefore has a finite basis by [F6]. Define
 $\Delta_{A^*}:=\theta_{A,A}^{-1}\circ m_A^*$ and $\varepsilon_{A^*}(f):=f(1_A)$.
For $f\in A^*$ and $a,b\in A$, evaluation through $\theta_{A,A}$ gives $\theta_{A,A}(\Delta_{A^*}f)(a\otimes b)=f(ab)$.
The tensor-product pairing on three finite-dimensional factors, obtained by applying [F3] twice and reassociating, separates elements of $A^*\otimes A^*\otimes A^*$.

For arbitrary coalgebra $C$, define convolution by [F5]. It is bilinear because $\Delta_C$ is linear and tensor evaluation is bilinear. For $f,g,h\in C^*$ and $c\in C$, the values $((f*g)*h)(c)$ and $(f*(g*h))(c)$ are evaluations of $f\otimes g\otimes h$ on $(\Delta_C\otimes\operatorname{id})\Delta_C(c)$ and $(\operatorname{id}\otimes\Delta_C)\Delta_C(c)$; coassociativity in [F2] makes them equal. The two counit equations give $(\varepsilon_C*f)(c)=f(c)=(f*\varepsilon_C)(c)$. Hence $C^*$ is a unital associative algebra, without a finite-dimensionality hypothesis on $C$.

Let $\psi:C\to D$ be a coalgebra map. For $f,g\in D^*$ and $c\in C$, $\psi^*(f*g)(c)=(f\otimes g)(\Delta_D(\psi(c)))=(f\otimes g)((\psi\otimes\psi)\Delta_C(c))=((\psi^*f)*(\psi^*g))(c)$. Also $\psi^*(\varepsilon_D)=\varepsilon_D\psi=\varepsilon_C$. Therefore $\psi^*:D^*\to C^*$ is a unital algebra map.

For finite-dimensional coalgebra $C$, [F6] gives a finite basis of $C$; define $\eta_C:C\to C^{**}$ by $\eta_C(c)(f)=f(c)$. A finite basis of $C$ and its dual show $\eta_C$ is a vector-space isomorphism. For $f,g\in C^*$, evaluating $\Delta_{C^{**}}\eta_C(c)$ against $f\otimes g$ gives $\eta_C(c)(f*g)=(f*g)(c)=(f\otimes g)(\Delta_C(c))$. The same evaluation of $(\eta_C\otimes\eta_C)\Delta_C(c)$ has that value; finite tensor duality [F3] therefore gives equality of the coproducts. Also $\varepsilon_{C^{**}}(\eta_C(c))=\eta_C(c)(\varepsilon_C)=\varepsilon_C(c)$. Hence $\eta_C$ is a coalgebra isomorphism.

For $a,b,c\in A$, evaluation of $(\Delta_{A^*}\otimes\operatorname{id})\Delta_{A^*}(f)$ on $a\otimes b\otimes c$ is $f((ab)c)$, while evaluation of $(\operatorname{id}\otimes\Delta_{A^*})\Delta_{A^*}(f)$ is $f(a(bc))$. These are equal by associativity in [F1]; separation from 1.1 gives coassociativity. Similarly, evaluation of $(\varepsilon_{A^*}\otimes\operatorname{id})\Delta_{A^*}(f)$ at $a$ is $f(1_Aa)=f(a)$ and evaluation of $(\operatorname{id}\otimes\varepsilon_{A^*})\Delta_{A^*}(f)$ at $a$ is $f(a1_A)=f(a)$. Thus both counit identities hold, so $A^*$ is a coalgebra.

Let $\phi:A\to B$ be a unital algebra map between finite-dimensional algebras, so [F6] supplies finite bases for both. Its transpose $\phi^*:B^*\to A^*$ preserves counits since $\varepsilon_{A^*}(\phi^*f)=f(\phi(1_A))=f(1_B)=\varepsilon_{B^*}(f)$. For $a,a'\in A$, evaluation of $\Delta_{A^*}(\phi^*f)$ at $a\otimes a'$ is $f(\phi(aa'))=f(\phi(a)\phi(a'))$. Writing $\Delta_{B^*}(f)=\sum_r f_r\otimes g_r$, evaluation of $(\phi^*\otimes\phi^*)\Delta_{B^*}(f)$ at $a\otimes a'$ is $\sum_r f_r(\phi(a))g_r(\phi(a'))=\Delta_{B^*}(f)(\phi(a)\otimes\phi(a'))=f(\phi(a)\phi(a'))$ by the defining transpose formula in 1.1. Since $A$ is finite-dimensional, [F3] separates the tensors, so $\phi^*$ is a coalgebra map.

For finite-dimensional $A$, [F6] supplies a finite basis; define $\eta_A:A\to A^{**}$ by $\eta_A(a)(f)=f(a)$. If $a_1,\dots,a_n$ is a basis and $a_1^*,\dots,a_n^*$ its dual basis, then $\eta_A(a_i)$ is the dual basis to $a_i^*$; hence $\eta_A$ is a vector-space isomorphism. For $f\in A^*$, convolution in $A^{**}$ and the defining equation for $\Delta_{A^*}$ give $(\eta_A(a)*\eta_A(b))(f)=\sum \eta_A(a)(f_1)\eta_A(b)(f_2)=\Delta_{A^*}(f)(a\otimes b)=f(ab)=\eta_A(ab)(f)$. The unit of $A^{**}$ is the counit of $A^*$, and its value on $f$ is $f(1_A)=\eta_A(1_A)(f)$. Thus $\eta_A$ is an algebra isomorphism.

For composable maps $u:V\to W$ and $v:W\to X$, precomposition gives $(v\circ u)^*=u^*\circ v^*$, so the transposes in steps 2.3 and 1.3 define contravariant functors. The evaluation maps are natural: for a linear map $u:V\to W$, $u^{**}(\eta_V(v))(f)=\eta_V(v)(f\circ u)=f(u(v))=\eta_W(u(v))(f)$. Steps 2.4 and 2.1 show these natural maps are structure-preserving isomorphisms on the finite subcategories, so the two dual functors are inverse equivalences there. The hypothesis concerns the whole algebra or coalgebra object; a finite-dimensional comodule over an infinite-dimensional coalgebra does not make that coalgebra finite-dimensional.

Steps 1.1 and 2.2 make $A^*$ a coalgebra when $A$ is finite; step 1.2 makes $C^*$ an algebra for every coalgebra; steps 2.3 and 1.3 prove reversal on algebra and coalgebra maps; steps 2.4, 2.1, and 3.1 prove the finite bidual equivalence and its scope.

$$
\rho_M:M\longrightarrow M\otimes C,
$$
such that
$$

A **Hopf algebra over $k$** is a bialgebra $H$ together with a $k$-linear map $S:H\to H$, called its **antipode**, such that

$$S*\mathrm{id}_H=u\varepsilon=\mathrm{id}_H*S,$$

where $*$ is the convolution product on $\operatorname{Hom}_k(H,H)$, $u:k\to H$ is the unit, and $\varepsilon:H\to k$ is the counit. Equivalently, $m(S\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta=u\varepsilon=m(\mathrm{id}\otimes S)\Delta$. Thus $S$ is the two-sided inverse of $\mathrm{id}_H$ in the convolution algebra. This definition imposes no compositional bijectivity condition on $S$.

For a finite-dimensional unital associative $k$-algebra $A$, the full dual $A^*$ is a coalgebra under the transpose of multiplication and unit. For every coalgebra $C$, the full dual $C^*$ is a unital associative algebra under convolution. These dualizations reverse algebra and coalgebra maps. Restricted to finite-dimensional objects, the two contravariant dualizations are inverse equivalences via the canonical evaluation maps $A\to A^{**}$ and $C\to C^{**}$. The finite-dimensionality hypothesis in the algebra-to-coalgebra direction is on $A$ itself, not merely on a module over $A$.

Let $V,W$ be finite-dimensional $k$-vector spaces.

1. The bilinear map $V^*\times W^*\to(V\otimes W)^*$, $(f,g)\mapsto[v\otimes w\mapsto f(v)g(w)]$, induces an isomorphism $V^*\otimes W^*\to(V\otimes W)^*$. For ordered bases $(v_1,\dots,v_m)$ of $V$, $(w_1,\dots,w_n)$ of $W$ with dual bases $(v_i^*)$, $(w_j^*)$, the image of $v_i^*\otimes w_j^*$ is the dual basis vector of $v_i\otimes w_j$ in the product basis of $V\otimes W$.
2. For every ordered basis $(v_1,\dots,v_n)$ of $V$ the element $\sum_{i=1}^nv_i^*\otimes v_i\in V^*\otimes V$ is independent of the basis and corresponds to $\mathrm{id}_V$ under the isomorphism $V^*\otimes V\to\operatorname{Hom}(V,V)$, $f\otimes v\mapsto[x\mapsto f(x)v]$ ([[thm-hom-from-a-finite-dimensional-space-as-a-tensor-product]]). Its image under $\sigma_{V^*,V}$ is the corresponding element $\sum_iv_i\otimes v_i^*$ of $V\otimes V^*$.
3. The evaluation $\mathrm{ev}:V^*\otimes V\to k$, $f\otimes v\mapsto f(v)$, and the coevaluation $\mathrm{coev}:k\to V\otimes V^*$, $1\mapsto\sum_iv_i\otimes v_i^*$, are independent of the basis and satisfy $(\mathrm{id}_V\otimes\mathrm{ev})\circ\alpha_{V,V^*,V}\circ(\mathrm{coev}\otimes\mathrm{id}_V)=\mathrm{id}_V$ and $(\mathrm{ev}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{V^*})\circ\alpha^{-1}_{V^*,V,V^*}\circ(\mathrm{id}_{V^*}\otimes\mathrm{coev})=\mathrm{id}_{V^*}$, the unit isomorphisms $k\otimes V\cong V$, $V\otimes k\cong V$ being understood.

Fix a field $k$. A **bialgebra over $k$** is a $k$-vector space $H$ with a unital associative $k$-algebra structure $(m,u)$ and a counital coassociative $k$-coalgebra structure $(\Delta,\varepsilon)$ in the sense of [[def-hh-coalgebra-and-coalgebra-map]], where $m:H\otimes H\to H$, $u:k\to H$, $\Delta:H\to H\otimes H$, and $\varepsilon:H\to k$. Explicitly, the algebra equations are $m(m\otimes\mathrm{id})=m(\mathrm{id}\otimes m)$ and $m(u\otimes\mathrm{id})=\mathrm{id}=m(\mathrm{id}\otimes u)$ under the canonical identifications; the coalgebra equations are those of [[def-hh-coalgebra-and-coalgebra-map]].

Require $\Delta:H\to H\otimes H$ and $\varepsilon:H\to k$ to be unital algebra homomorphisms. The algebra on $H\otimes H$ is the one with $(a\otimes b)(c\otimes d)=ac\otimes bd$ and unit $1_H\otimes1_H$; the algebra on $k$ is its field algebra. A **bialgebra map** $f:H\to K$ is a $k$-linear map preserving multiplication, unit, comultiplication, and counit: $f m_H=m_K(f\otimes f)$, $fu_H=u_K$, $\Delta_Kf=(f\otimes f)\Delta_H$, and $\varepsilon_Kf=\varepsilon_H$.

For a fixed comultiplication $\Delta:C\to C\otimes C$, there is at most one counit. Also, Sweedler notation records a finite tensor sum, not a list of canonical summands: every contraction written from that notation must be the value of a well-defined linear map on the tensor.

The same finite tensor duality for $H\otimes H$ permits transposing every structural identity in [F1] and [F2].

The convolution product on $H^*$ is associative: evaluating $(\phi\psi)\theta$ and $\phi(\psi\theta)$ on $h$ gives respectively $\sum\phi(h_1)\psi(h_2)\theta(h_3)$ through the two iterated coproducts of $H$, which agree by coassociativity; the counit identities make $\varepsilon$ its left and right unit.

The coproduct $m^*$ on $H^*$ is coassociative because evaluating $(m^*\otimes\mathrm{id})m^*(\phi)$ and $(\mathrm{id}\otimes m^*)m^*(\phi)$ on $a\otimes b\otimes c$ gives $\phi((ab)c)$ and $\phi(a(bc))$, equal by associativity of $H$; evaluation at $1_H$ is a two-sided counit by $1_Ha=a=a1_H$.

The coproduct on $H^*$ preserves convolution products: for $\phi,\psi\in H^*$ and $a,b\in H$, $\Delta_{H^*}(\phi\psi)(a\otimes b) =(\phi\psi)(ab) =\sum \phi(a_1b_1)\psi(a_2b_2) =\bigl(\Delta_{H^*}(\phi)\Delta_{H^*}(\psi)\bigr)(a\otimes b),$ where the second equality uses that $\Delta_H$ is an algebra map. The unit $\varepsilon_H$ is group-like for $\Delta_{H^*}$, since $\varepsilon_H(ab)=\varepsilon_H(a)\varepsilon_H(b)$; the counit $\phi\mapsto\phi(1_H)$ preserves convolution products because $\Delta_H(1_H)=1_H\otimes1_H$. Thus the maps in the Statement make $H^*$ a bialgebra.

Define $S^*(\phi)=\phi\circ S$. Likewise, $\bigl(\phi_{(1)}S^*(\phi_{(2)})\bigr)(h) =\sum_{(h),i}\phi_i(h_1)\psi_i(S(h_2)) =\sum_{(h)}\phi(h_1S(h_2)) =\varepsilon(h)\phi(1_H),$ using the right antipode equation in [F1]. Both convolution equations hold, so $S^*$ is an antipode on $H^*$, and no step uses $S^{-1}$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $S$ a set. There is a unital associative $R$-algebra $R\langle S\rangle$, the **free associative $R$-algebra on $S$**, whose underlying $R$-module is free on the set of finite words in $S$ (including the empty word), with product given on words by concatenation and extended $R$-bilinearly.

1. **Universal property.** For every $R$-algebra $A$ ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) and every map $S\to A$ there is a unique unital $R$-algebra homomorphism $R\langle S\rangle\to A$ extending it. When $R=k$ is a field and $S$ indexes a basis of a vector space $V$, $R\langle S\rangle$ reproduces the published tensor algebra $T(V)$ ([[def-tensor-algebra-of-a-vector-space]], [[thm-universal-property-of-the-tensor-algebra]]).
2. **Two-sided ideal description.** For $E\subseteq R\langle S\rangle$ the two-sided ideal $(E)$ ([[def-generated-and-principal-ideals]]) is the set of finite sums $\sum_sa_se_sb_s$ with $a_s,b_s\in R\langle S\rangle$ and $e_s\in E$.
3. **Quotient universal property.** If $\varphi:R\langle S\rangle\to A$ is an $R$-algebra homomorphism killing $E$, then $\varphi$ factors uniquely through the quotient $R\langle S\rangle/(E)$ ([[thm-quotient-ring-universal-property]]); the quotient is the presented $R$-algebra with generators $S$ and relations $E$.

Fix the following conventions, used on this page and by the later Hopf and Hecke pages.

- For an algebra $A$ over a commutative ring ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) the opposite algebra $A^{\mathrm{op}}$ has the same underlying set and structure map and product $a\cdot b:=ba$ ([[def-opposite-ring]]).
- Finite sums $\sum_{i\in I}x_i$ follow [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]; an empty sum is $0$.

Parentheses in iterated tensor products may be dropped only after [[lem-hh-tensor-coherence-on-elementary-tensors]] has been proved.

Let $k$ be a field and let $L,M,N,X$ be $k$-vector spaces. Write $\alpha_{A,B,C}:(A\otimes B)\otimes C\to A\otimes(B\otimes C)$ for the associators of [[thm-symmetry-and-associativity-over-a-commutative-ring]], $\sigma_{A,B}$ for its symmetries, and $\lambda,\rho$ for the unit isomorphisms of [[thm-unit-isomorphisms-for-module-tensor-products]].

derivations.claim: Let $T$ be the vector space with basis $e_{i,j}$, $i\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$, $0\le j<N$, and extend bilinearly the rule $e_{i,j}e_{a,b}=\zeta^{-aj}e_{i+a,j+b}$ when $j+b<N$, and $0$ otherwise. For a triple of basis elements, if $j+b+d\ge N$, both parenthesizations vanish: if an intermediate degree reaches $N$ it is truncated, and otherwise the final multiplication truncates. If $j+b+d<N$, the scalar in $(e_{i,j}e_{a,b})e_{c,d}$ is $\zeta^{-aj-c(j+b)}$, while the scalar in $e_{i,j}(e_{a,b}e_{c,d})$ is $\zeta^{-cb-(a+c)j}$; these exponents are equal, and both outputs are $e_{i+a+c,j+b+d}$. Hence multiplication is associative by bilinearity, and $e_{0,0}$ is its two-sided unit.

Put $g=e_{1,0}$ and $x=e_{0,1}$. The formula gives $g^N=e_{0,0}$, $x^N=0$, $gx=e_{1,1}$, and $xg=\zeta^{-1}e_{1,1}$, so $gx=\zeta xg$. Thus the relations define a surjective algebra map from the presented quotient $Q=k\langle g,x\rangle/(g^N-1,x^N,gx-\zeta xg)$ to $T$, since each $e_{i,j}$ is the image of $g^i x^j$, by [F2].

In $Q$, the relation $xg=\zeta^{-1}gx$ moves every $g$ to the left of every $x$; reducing $g$-powers modulo $N$ and setting any $x$-power at least $N$ to zero shows that the $N^2$ words $g^i x^j$, $0\le i,j<N$, span $Q$. Their images in $T$ are its distinct basis vectors $e_{i,j}$, hence are linearly independent in $Q$ as well. Therefore $Q\to T$ is an isomorphism and the claimed PBW basis is valid.

Define $\Delta$ on the free algebra by the stated generator images. They preserve the relations: $\Delta(g)^N=1$, and with $A=1\otimes x$, $B=x\otimes g$ one has $BA=\zeta AB$ and $\Delta(x)=A+B$. If $(A+B)^n=\sum_{r=0}^n C_{n,r}A^{n-r}B^r$, then $C_{0,0}=1$ and $C_{n+1,r}=\zeta^rC_{n,r}+C_{n,r-1}$, since $B^rA=\zeta^rAB^r$. For $0\le n<N$ and $0\le r\le n$, the recurrence gives $C_{n,r}=\prod_{s=1}^r(1-\zeta^{n-r+s})/(1-\zeta^s)$: for $1\le r\le n$, set $P=\prod_{s=1}^{r-1}(1-\zeta^{n-r+1+s})$ and $D=\prod_{s=1}^r(1-\zeta^s)$; then $C_{n,r}=P(1-\zeta^{n-r+1})/D$ and $C_{n,r-1}=P(1-\zeta^r)/D$, so $\zeta^rC_{n,r}+C_{n,r-1}=P(1-\zeta^{n+1})/D=C_{n+1,r}$. For $n=N$ and $0<r<N$, the same formula has nonzero denominator factors and a numerator factor $1-\zeta^N=0$; hence $(A+B)^N=A^N+B^N=0$. Also $\Delta(g)\Delta(x)=g\otimes gx+gx\otimes g^2=\zeta(g\otimes xg+xg\otimes g^2)=\zeta\Delta(x)\Delta(g)$, so $\Delta(gx-\zeta xg)=0$, and $\Delta$ descends to $Q$.

Extend $S$ as an anti-algebra map from the free algebra using $S(g)=g^{-1}$ and $S(x)=-xg^{-1}$. The relation ideal is killed: $S(g^N-1)=g^{-N}-1=0$; reordering with $g^{-1}x=\zeta^{-1}xg^{-1}$ shows $S(x^N)=(-xg^{-1})^N$ is a scalar multiple of $x^Ng^{-N}=0$; and $S(gx-\zeta xg)=S(x)S(g)-\zeta S(g)S(x)=-xg^{-2}+\zeta g^{-1}xg^{-1}=0$. Thus $S$ descends to $Q$.

The assignment $\varepsilon(g)=1,\varepsilon(x)=0$ kills $g^N-1$, $x^N$, and $gx-\zeta xg$, so it descends to an algebra map $Q\to k$. Coassociativity holds on $g$ immediately; on $x$, both iterates equal $1\otimes1\otimes x+1\otimes x\otimes g+x\otimes g\otimes g$. The two counit equations hold on $g,x$ by the given values. These maps are algebra maps, and the presented algebra is generated by $g,x$, so the identities extend to all of $Q$.

On $g$, both $m(S\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta$ and $m(\mathrm{id}\otimes S)\Delta$ give $1=\varepsilon(g)1$. On $x$, the left product is $x+(-xg^{-1})g=0$, and the right product is $-xg^{-1}+xg^{-1}=0=\varepsilon(x)1$. For products $ab$ of elements on which both identities hold, anti-multiplicativity of $S$ and multiplicativity of $\Delta$ give $\sum S(a_1b_1)a_2b_2=\sum S(b_1)(S(a_1)a_2)b_2=\varepsilon(a)\varepsilon(b)1$, and $\sum a_1b_1S(a_2b_2)=\sum a_1(b_1S(b_2))S(a_2)=\varepsilon(a)\varepsilon(b)1$. Induction on word length and linearity extend both antipode equations to all of $Q$. Thus the given maps make $Q$ a Hopf algebra, with the interface of [F1].
